newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus, Rsusian leaders urge faster integration.
newsitem.headline: Belarus, Rsusian leaders urge faster integration.

text.p: Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko and Russian President Boris Yeltsin urged the parliaments of their two countries on Tuesday to help speed up moves towards closer integration.
Lukashenko made his appeal at a parliamentary assembly of 25 deputies from each of the neighbouring Slav states, to which the Kremlin said Yeltsin had sent a written message.

"I propose that you, energetically and quickly, concentrate on approving a citizenship (law) of the community," Lukashenko said in a speech underlining Belarus' determination to maintain its territorial integrity despite its desire for closer ties.

"Every citizen of Russia and Belarus is a citizen of the community and of his own country...This will secure freedom of movement, equal citizens' rights in the two states and equal participation in elections," he said.

Yeltsin said much work had been done since he and Lukashenko signed a pact on forming an economic "community" between Belarus and Russia last April, but it was now time to speed the process up and move from declarations to action.
"I am sure the parliamentary assembly will give a new dynamism to integration between Russia and Belarus," Yeltsin said in his message, published by the Kremlin.

Lukashenko repeated criticism of Russia, a country of about 150 million people, for slow progress in moves in the last year towards integration with Belarus -- its small western neighbour with a population of about 10 million.
"Today I propose to Russia: let us create a union following the formula of two states, two voices. But Russia is not ready for this," he said to applause from Russian deputies.

Lukashenko met Yeltsin in Moscow last Friday and the two leaders signed a declaration that called for integration of their customs, fiscal, transport and energy systems and synchronisation of economic reforms.
Lukashenko's slow approach to reform has led to international lending bodies suspending credits to Belarus.
His policy of forming some kind of union with Russia helped to put him in power although it is opposed by a noisy sector who accuse him of ignoring democratic principles to shore up his leadership.
The latest protest against his policies on Monday ended in angry scuffles with police, at least two injuries and about 100 arrests, opposition leaders said.
In typically critical comments on Western plans to expand the NATO alliance eastwards, Lukashenko said an alternative alliance could be set up between China, Russia and Belarus.

"We have discussed the possibility with the Chinese leadership of a Beijing-Moscow-Minsk axis. This would be a strategic axis, an air corridor, our answer to NATO expansion. We can find many answers," he said.
Russia and China, who seek to improve political and economic ties, have rejected any idea of forming a military bloc.
Lukashenko, who once called NATO a monster, accused the West of setting up electronic intelligence monitoring equipment on the Polish and Lithuanian borders of his former Soviet republic.
